The **Holborn 9100** was a personal computer introduced in 1981 by a small [Dutch](/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands") company called [Holborn](/w/index.php?title=Holborn_(company)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Holborn (company) (page does not exist)") [[nl](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holborn_(bedrijf) "nl:Holborn (bedrijf)")]. Only around 200 of these devices were sold, with Holborn going into [bankruptcy](/wiki/Bankruptcy "Bankruptcy") in 1983.

title: Holborn 9100
text:
## History

The Holborn 9100 was released in 1981 by Dutch computer manufacturer Holborn. The appearance was designed by an industrial design office named Studio Vos and developed by Hans Polak and Henny Beavers. The name comes from the phrase "born in Holland." There were two main versions, a larger one with a proprietary multi-user operating system named Holborn OS with support for a [light pen](/wiki/Light_pen "Light pen"), and a smaller machine with the operating system [CP/M](/wiki/CP/M "CP/M") and no light pen support.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)

These versions were split into four different models released: the 9100, 7100, 6500, and 6100. The systems consist primarily of a combined desktop [monitor](/wiki/Computer_monitor "Computer monitor"), [terminal](/wiki/Computer_terminal "Computer terminal"), and [keyboard](/wiki/Computer_keyboard "Computer keyboard") with an external unit housing two 8 inch [floppy drives](/wiki/Floppy_drives "Floppy drives") and an optional [hard drive](/wiki/Hard_disk_drive "Hard disk drive"). The 6500 series had a detachable keyboard.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) The computer was primarily marketed to small companies for administration and bookkeeping purposes.[[2]](#cite_note-:1-2) The lower-numbered models were produced after the release of the 9100.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) Around 200 machines were produced, with 50 of them being the larger models.[[2]](#cite_note-:1-2)

These versions were split into four different models released: the 9100, 7100, 6500, and 6100. The systems consist primarily of a combined desktop [monitor](/wiki/Computer_monitor "Computer monitor"), [terminal](/wiki/Computer_terminal "Computer terminal"), and [keyboard](/wiki/Computer_keyboard "Computer keyboard") with an external unit housing two 8 inch [floppy drives](/wiki/Floppy_drives "Floppy drives") and an optional [hard drive](/wiki/Hard_disk_drive "Hard disk drive"). The 6500 series had a detachable keyboard.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) The computer was primarily marketed to small companies for administration and bookkeeping purposes.[[2]](#cite_note-:1-2) The lower-numbered models were produced after the release of the 9100.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) Around 200 machines were produced, with 50 of them being the larger models.[[2]](#cite_note-:1-2)

Due to the high price of the system at the time at 30,000 [guilder](/wiki/Dutch_guilder "Dutch guilder")[[3]](#cite_note-3) or $10,000 USD (equivalent to $30,591 in 2023) and competition from [IBM](/wiki/IBM "IBM"), the system was a commercial failure and caused the manufacturer to go bankrupt in 1983. The most popular version was the 6100.[[4]](#cite_note-:2-4) It is estimated that around 20 systems survive.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)

## Specifications

- OS: Holborn OS or [CP/M](/wiki/CP/M "CP/M")
- CPU: [Zilog Z80A](/wiki/Zilog_Z80 "Zilog Z80") at 4 MHz
- RAM: 72 KB (expandable to 220KB)
- Storage: 2.5 MB on two 8 inch floppy disks, optional 30 MB hard drive
- Monitor: 12 inch, made of green [phosphors](/wiki/Phosphor "Phosphor")

title: Holborn 9100
text:
## Holborn OS

Holborn OS (HOS) was a multi-user [operating system](/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system") developed by Holborn. It was stored entirely on [ROM](/wiki/ROM "ROM") and used floppy disks to start applications.[[5]](#cite_note-:3-5) The application software was menu driven and could be controlled by a light pen to aid use by technically unskilled users.[[6]](#cite_note-:4-6)

title: Holborn 9100
text:
## Holborn

Holborn Computers was founded in 1979 by Hans Polak and Dick Gerdzen. The goal of the company was to supply computers based on [microprocessor](/wiki/Microprocessor "Microprocessor") technology to specific types of retailers.[[6]](#cite_note-:4-6) The company saw a market for cheaper computer systems as IBM computers were expensive at the time. Henny Beavers joined soon afterwards. The company aimed to design and manufacture the systems as quickly as possible to get them out in the market.[[5]](#cite_note-:3-5)

Once the Holborn 9100 was released in 1981, they marketed it using displays at [trade shows](/wiki/Trade_show "Trade show") and advertisements. Due to competition from more popular IBM computers, Holborn remained dependent on financial aid from the [Overijssel](/wiki/Overijssel "Overijssel") development company OOM.[[5]](#cite_note-:3-5) OOM could not supply enough financial resources and Gerdzen had to leave the company, causing the company to go bankrupt on 27 April 1983. They ultimately considered the 9100 a failure.[[4]](#cite_note-:2-4)

title: Holborn 9100
text:
## Reception

The Holborn 9100 is noted for its design, being referred to as "something out of a [retro-futuristic](/wiki/Retrofuturism "Retrofuturism") movie" by cybernews.[[7]](#cite_note-7) Inexhibit noted that "The design of the Holborn set it apart from most computers of the time," calling it futuristic and organic.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)
